header:
Date: 2026-09-24 | Start: 16:00 PDT | Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Connor Hayes (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Lead ML Infra, Pangea), Marcus Chen (Platform Eng, Pangea), Priya Rao (CTO, Pangea)
summary: Deep dive into KV cache tearout, paging behavior on long-context workloads, and prefetch strategies. Discussed hot-prefix detection, eviction hysteresis, async prefetch, and trade-offs between memory footprint and latency. Agreed next steps to share telemetry, run synthetic replay with prefix-affinity, and review VPC/on-prem security checklist. Pangea concerned about spill-to-disk latency spikes during bursty sessions and prefix reuse across multi-tenant routing.
topics: Observed tail-latency spikes during 10k token sessions
KV eviction patterns and prefix collisions
Paging to local NVMe vs remote S3 spillback
Quantization impact on memory and eviction frequency
VPC/on-prem telemetry and audit log requirements
transcript:
00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thank you for joining, this is Maya from Redwood. We ran a quick agenda — Connor will walk through the runtime traces then we can dig into the eviction and your hot prefix patterns.
00:18 Connor: Hey, hi — thanks. I pulled the last 72 hours of traces you shared, Lena, and there are a few things that stand out. There's a collection of mid-tail latency spikes that correlate with KV spill events — when the session store loses prefix residency and has to page back in.
00:35 Lena: Yeah, that's the stuff we saw. We call them "long sessions" but they're really multiple contiguous contexts — like a 8k to 12k token stitch — and then sometimes they burst with many short follow-ups.
00:50 Marcus: One thing to note, our infra is multitenant, and the prefix reuse is pretty aggressive — different agents re-use similar conversational prefixes. We think that might be causing some eviction churn.
01:05 Connor: Right, prefix reuse across tenants will create hot-set contention. In the traces I see short TTLs on some entries and immediate eviction — looks like a simple LRU that's being thrash-killed by a few noisy prefixes.
01:20 Priya: Quick clarification — when you say TTLs on entries, you mean the runtime's per-prefix residency time, not a global token TTL?
01:28 Connor: Exactly. The runtime maintains per-prefix residency with an eviction policy, and we also have heuristics for keeping recent K-Vs around. But with long-context streaming, the KV footprint per session balloons and pushes cold prefixes out.
01:44 Maya: Can I back up — Marcus, what's your memory budget per GPU for session-state? Are you using Dedicated or our hosted mode?
01:52 Marcus: We're trying Redwood Hosted at the moment, with a soft cap of 48GB per instance for KV.

02:03 Connor: 48 gigs is fine for many workloads, but with 12k token contexts on average, the effective per-session KV grows. Also, quantized weights help model memory but KV is orthogonal — it's token-level state.
02:18 Lena: We also observed some cases where the runtime paged to NVMe and latencies shot up to 700–900ms on first token after a spill. That kills our UX.
02:30 Connor: Yeah, the spillback path matters. Spilling to local NVMe is faster than remote object store, but still non-trivial. For those first-token spikes, there are two levers: proactive prefetch (warm the KV before the token is needed) or async-other-thread fetch with immediate approximate decoding.
02:48 Maya: We wanted to cover prefetch heuristics — what we've done on Redwood is a few strategies: stride-based prefetch for sequential token consumption, prefix-affinity where we warm related keys when a known prefix is detected, and a small hotset pinning for very high-frequency prefixes.
03:05 Marcus: Can stride work with chat that has many short jumps? Often the UX has users jump between threads.
03:12 Connor: Stride alone fails with random-access patterns. That's why prefix-affinity is usually paired with a cheap similarity check — if we detect the session is re-using a previous prefix (fuzzy hash), we warm that prefix. For your multi-tenant case, noisy tenants can still evict others unless we isolate hot tenants with reserved slabs.
03:35 Lena: Reserved slabs? Can you explain—like fixed memory partitions per tenant?
03:40 Connor: Kind of. A slab allocator can reserve a fraction of KV memory per tenant or per prefix-group, preventing full global thrash. The tradeoff is unused reserved memory if the tenant's load is light. But it prevents neighbor-induced evictions.
03:54 Priya: We're concerned about cost — reserved slabs sound expensive. Any dynamic alternatives?
03:58 Connor: Sure: adaptive quota where the system tracks per-tenant miss rate and grants extra slab when misses exceed a threshold, with a decay back to default. It's a middle ground — not hard reservation but throttled weight.
04:12 Marcus: About eviction hysteresis — is that something you can tune? We're seeing immediate evictions after a small spike.
04:18 Connor: Yes, eviction hysteresis adds a grace window — rather than evicting on first pressure signal, we only evict if pressure persists for X seconds or after Y allocations. This reduces ping-ponging hot prefixes. In our tests we saw 20–40% reduction in repeat fetches with a 10s hysteresis.
04:35 Lena: Interesting. About quantization — we tried 4-bit and it reduced runtime memory but increased CPU decode time slightly. But I didn't expect it to affect KV eviction.
04:45 Connor: It shouldn't directly, but model-level changes change per-token latency and throughput and therefore request concurrency, which changes effective KV footprints. If quant reduces model memory and you increase batch sizes, KV pressure can go up if more sessions are kept warm concurrently.
04:59 Maya: Let's talk about telemetry — Connor, what telemetry did you request?
05:03 Connor: Per-prefix metrics: size, last-access, hit/miss rate, eviction count, spill count (NVMe vs S3), and correlation to request id and tenant. Also histogram of first-token latency post-spill. If you can dump a CSV for last 72h, that helps us simulate.
05:18 Lena: We can provide that. I think we already sent a limited set, but we'll include per-prefix hitstreams.
05:25 Marcus: One of our scary patterns — prefix collisions where semantically orthogonal prefixes hash to the same slot and evict each other in the slab. Any mitigation?
05:35 Connor: Hash collisions are rare if you use a good hash; but slot-based allocators can degrade if prefix mapping is skewed. Solutions: increase associativity (multi-way set), use content-aware placement, or a small secondary cache with content-addressable placement.
05:50 Priya: How about paging strategies — local NVMe vs remote? We want to avoid remote S3 for tail reads but can't afford unlimited NVMe.
05:59 Connor: You can tier: keep most-frequently-used on memory, overflow to local NVMe with async prefetch, and only spill coldest to remote object store as a last resort. Also keep a compacted summary on remote to enable partial warm of indices.
06:15 Lena: I saw in the traces that compaction was happening every 10 minutes and that coincided with small spikes. Is compaction synchronous?
06:22 Connor: In your cluster it looked synchronous — that's a configuration we can change. Make compaction incremental and non-blocking; run slab compaction in background with rate limits so it doesn't interfere with hotpath IO.
06:35 Marcus: Any good heuristics on what to prefetch when you detect a prefix? We worry about over-prefetch causing extra evictions.

06:42 Connor: The minimal approach: prefetch only immediate neighbors — tokens that are most likely requested (lookahead 1–2). Add adaptive budget per prefix: if the prefix's hit rate after prefetch is high, expand budget. If low, reduce. Also use sampling to avoid blindly warming everything.
06:58 Maya: Also a small trick — warm only metadata first (embedding/summary) rather than full KV payload; if the summary indicates likely reuse, then fetch full payload. Saves IO.
07:12 Lena: That could help. We have partial metadata per prefix.
07:16 Priya: What about concurrency controls — if we get a thundering herd for a single hot prefix?
07:22 Connor: Strongly recommend request coalescing: one background fetch services N waiting requests. Use in-flight request dedupe and fan-out response. Also rate-limit background prefetch to avoid sudden IO storms.
07:36 Marcus: Ok, question about metrics — you mentioned first-token latency spike histogram. What thresholds are realistic? We're trying to keep p95 under 200ms and p99 under 400ms.
07:47 Connor: With local NVMe and good prefetch you can hit those numbers. If spill goes to remote object store, p99 easily crosses 1s. So aim to keep first-token after spill < 350ms by warming NVMe or avoiding the spill entirely.
07:59 Maya: Let's walk through a proposed short-term remediation plan: 1) identify top 200 hot prefixes and pin them, 2) enable 10s eviction hysteresis, 3) change compaction to async, 4) enable request coalescing and small-lookahead prefetch. Any objections?
08:18 Priya: Sounds reasonable — we just want to measure cost impact. How much memory will pinning 200 prefixes use?
08:25 Connor: Depends on prefix size. If median prefix is 80KB, 200 prefixes is ~16MB — negligible. The problem is if some prefixes are huge (MBs). So we need prefix size distribution.
08:36 Lena: We'll include distribution in the telemetry dump.
08:39 Maya: Great. Another angle — routing and isolation. If you can route high-risk tenants to a dedicated pool (Dedicated RDW) with reserved capacity, it simplifies.
08:50 Marcus: There's procurement and cost hurdles for Dedicated, but for a pilot we can try a small reserved pool.
08:56 Connor: For the pilot, we recommend 2–3 GPUs dedicated with reserved slab and quantized model to control model memory; that isolates KV dynamics.
09:06 Priya: On VPC/on-prem — we need to see audit logs and KMS integration. Maya, can you share the security checklist?
09:13 Maya: Yes, I'll share the VPC/on-prem checklist and SOC artifacts — that'll be in the next steps.
09:18 Lena: Back to prefetch — what about predictive prefetch using a small LSTM or lightweight model to score likely next prefixes? Is that overkill?

09:26 Connor: It's doable and sometimes pays off — a tiny predictor trained on session transitions can reduce unnecessary prefetch by 30%. The cost is model maintenance and retraining. For many customers, a rules-based adaptive approach is simpler to start with.
09:40 Marcus: We also saw bursts during nightly batch jobs where many sessions get long replays which wipes the hotset. Any guardrails?

09:48 Connor: Yes: schedule compaction and heavy batch replays in off-peak windows and mark batch jobs as low-priority for background IO. Also set a sliding window that prevents batch-driven evictions from targeting realtime latency-critical shards.
10:02 Priya: I want to drill into one concrete trace — Connor, you flagged a specific request id where there was a 820ms spike and then eviction cascade. Can you talk through that quickly?
10:11 Connor: Sure — trace: request 0xA3F... the session had multiple prefixes across tenants. At t+0 it required prefix P1 which had been evicted 3s earlier. The runtime fetched P1 from NVMe (420ms), during that fetch other requests referenced P2 and P3 causing them to be queued; P2's background fetch attempted to prefetch P4 which triggered compaction, compaction blocked and caused additional GC which stalled the worker thread — chain reaction.
10:34 Lena: That compaction blocking is the scary bit — can we set compaction to only run on underutilized nodes?
10:40 Connor: Yes, or spawn it on separate threads with CPU affinity and IO capping. Non-blocking compaction will avoid blocking request threads.
10:48 Maya: We're already 10 minutes in — do you want to switch to the live telemetry now? Connor, I think you mentioned you'd share a dashboard snapshot.

10:55 Connor: Yep — I have a compact CSV I can drop in the notes. It shows per-prefix hit/miss and average eviction interval. But since this is a recorded call, I'll highlight the patterns: 1) 12 prefixes caused 60% of evictions, 2) top 5 tenants account for 70% of KV residency, 3) spill events correlate with 1.8x concurrency increases.
11:18 Marcus: Can we enable per-tenant soft caps so that these 5 tenants can't monopolize?
11:22 Connor: Yes, soft caps with auto-escalation when latency targets are met is a good pattern.
11:28 Lena: A quick tangent — what about using quantization to reduce KV pressure by reducing the model's tokenization overhead? Seems indirect.

11:36 Connor: It's indirect: quantization reduces model memory allowing more concurrent sessions per GPU, which increases total KV demand. So sometimes quantization increases aggregate KV pressure unless you're also increasing total overall memory footprint or isolating jobs. It's a balancing act.
11:50 Priya: Could Redwood runtime provide a simulator to predict eviction behavior before we change production configurations?
11:57 Connor: We have a lightweight simulator that replays traces and can model eviction and prefetch heuristics. It's not 100% accurate but very useful for comparative testing. We'll run it on your 48h trace once we get the CSV.
12:08 Maya: OK, let's try to map out the experiment matrix: baseline replay, enable eviction hysteresis, pin top-200 prefixes, enable prefetch with small lookahead, and then full pilot with dedicated pool. We'll compare p95/p99 first-token latencies and cost.
12:25 Marcus: Sounds good. Any immediate blockers for implementing hysteresis and coalescing?
12:30 Connor: No blockers — hysteresis is a config flip in our runtime, coalescing requires a small change to request path but it's low-risk. Prefetch tune needs telemetry to set budgets correctly.
12:42 Lena: Can you explain the prefix similarity fuzzy hash? Ours are sometimes similar but not identical because of slot markers.

12:49 Connor: Common approach: normalize prefixes (remove slot tokens, normalize punctuation), compute a locality-sensitive hash on tokens or embeddings, and then treat hashes within a small edit-distance as same-hot group. It isn't perfect but catches most reuse.
13:03 Priya: If we normalize aggressively we might merge unrelated prefixes — that could cause bad warms.

13:08 Connor: Correct. So we use a conservative threshold to start and increase if hit-rate suggests we're missing reuse. Keep monitoring.
13:17 Maya: We're at ~40 minutes, want to cover paging policies and the long-context stitch edge case quickly?
13:24 Connor: Long-context stitch — when you concatenate prior sessions into one larger context, KV keys for earlier segments are colder but still referenced. For that, consider hierarchical caching: keep recent segment KV in L1, older segments in L2 with faster escalator if they're re-referenced. Also compact old segments into a smaller summary to reduce footprint.
13:46 Marcus: Does Redwood support hierarchical KV out of the box?
13:49 Connor: We have a tiered option — default is single-level with NVMe spill, but tiered (in-memory L1 + compressed L2 on NVMe + cold object store) is an advanced config. We can enable it for your pilot.
13:59 Lena: On the subject of compression — is it CPU heavy to compress KVs? We're worried about CPU spikes.

14:06 Connor: Compression adds CPU but you can pick fast codecs (e.g., LZ4) with low CPU cost. Also do compression asynchronously on background threads to avoid request path CPU spikes.
14:18 Priya: Any gotchas with encrypted NVMe and KMS? We have strict compliance needs.

14:24 Maya: We've done customers with encrypted local disks and HSM-backed KMS; that increases latency a little for first write but reads are local and fast. We'll include the KMS integration doc in the security packet.
14:36 Marcus: How do you recommend we instrument to quickly detect prefix collisions?
14:42 Connor: Emit per-slot collision counts and per-prefix mapping histograms. If you see a small slot with many unique prefixes mapping, it's a collision hotspot. Also monitor evictions per slot.
14:55 Lena: Great. We're almost at the end — any final quick wins?
15:00 Connor: Quick wins: 1) Enable hysteresis (config flip), 2) make compaction non-blocking, 3) turn on request coalescing, 4) pin top N hot prefixes, 5) sample prefetch with a small lookahead. All low-code and we can help roll them out in a pilot.
15:18 Maya: Awesome. We'll capture these in next steps. Thanks everyone.
15:22 Priya: Thanks — appreciate the thoroughness.
15:25 Marcus: Thanks, talk soon.
15:28 Lena: Thanks all.
15:30 [meeting end]
